choristers around the excavation. By day it is the Sayers' dig (the story: 'A Sayer camp digs here and argues'); after dark the choristers come and stand round it and hold the note at it, which is what the knight in the Headless Watch warns you of.
swarm; they only rise if you touch the cup

a fallen Tolling knight on the stair if the watch has turned; otherwise a friendly vigil. The watch has turned while the Order's fallen are standing the north walk: from the Names in the Chapter Book's walk out to it until the book is answered. Otherwise only Calen Ash keeps the eye.
a bell-bearer at the top rings when it sees you: on the shelf of the lip, beside the glass

Ash-wights come in on the night flood and stand in the Tide Mouth until the ebb.
the miller and his boy at the stones, feeding ash between them; they mind the mill and nothing else, until somebody stops the sails or takes from the hopper. A sack of the grinding lies by the door.
the Hallows at the plough, four of them, ploughing the last furrow; they leave you be until you stand in their way. Their seed-bag lies in the barn.
a chorister walks the rows at dusk and sings the names off the bells; the burial list is tied round a bell-post
after dark the choristers come up out of the Under-Choir and stand round the headframe, holding the note down the shaft
on the nights with no moon a chorister stands in the lamp-socket with its mouth to the sea, holding the note; the note is the light the Salt Isles ships see (The Harbour Light)
ash-wights come to the coin-bowl after dark and take the pilgrims' coins, one each, and walk south with them towards the Stair
at dusk ash-wights walk the Builders' road west past the milestones, counting down to a harbour, and turn back at the last one
at night ash-wights come up the cistern stair out of the dry dark, wet to the knees
the strand-scavengers' book of what the sea brought in, on the driftwood table
a year's count, scored through, left on a stone for whoever wants it
the Gauge's reading-book, its chain cut, on the step
the price-board off the gate-post
ash-wights stand in the forecourt after dark, facing the door, listening

after dark ash-wights come out of the ash and stand on the hour-stones, one to a stone, as if waiting to be counted (Wenna Thrope's 'the night').
sleepers who wandered out of the head's mouth after dark, grey, going about an evening a hundred and seventy years old.
a chorister at the glass after dusk, looking at nothing in it; a pilgrim's note under a stone at its foot.
the moth-wife's count chalked on a slate at the end of a rack.
